scoring.note: Each fresh judge scored all four arms. Missing responses are represented in the panel and receive 1 under the rubric; missing-arm scores are never imputed by this script.

cohorts.original: References in the saved Round 3 panel keys, scored again by the fresh Round 4 judges.
cohorts.expanded: AI-written implementation references in the Round 4 panel keys, filtered by the authored Adobe requirement kind where a key exists, including missing no-AI responses.

weighting.pooled_question_weighted: Each scored requirement has equal weight across all RFIs.
weighting.equal_rfi_mean: Compute each RFI mean first, then give each RFI equal weight.

judge_notes: All 96 answers fit their stated word limits; brevity did not compensate for missing requested scope.
The strongest responses name the client systems, define concrete deliverables and include validation, while several weaker responses substitute product descriptions or adjacent services.
Planning estimates are common, but few answers establish calendar milestones against the ten month website and twelve month analytics commitments.
Several answers introduce separately licensed products or assume existing configurations despite the RFP stating that the selected products are not set up.

Adobe capability statements were judged for internal credibility without external verification; uncertain integration promises received less credit than explicit constraints and tested acceptance plans.
All 56 answers fit the stated word limit; brevity alone does not compensate for missing method or commitments.
Specific checks, signoffs, scoped deliverables and dependency based timing carry more weight than generic promises to agree details later.
Several answers promise artifacts in their deliverables without explaining the work that produces or validates them.

Universal Editor assumptions alongside Core Components and editable templates need a clearer compatible implementation, and analyst training should not introduce an unnecessary Adobe Analytics license dependency.
The strongest responses use Tallgrass's store, loyalty, Snowflake and authoring circumstances to shape the work; repeated channel descriptions add little evidence.
All 64 responses fall within their stated 250 word limits; brevity does not compensate for missing requirement coverage.
The strongest responses explain observable controls and acceptance evidence, while several weaker responses merely name deliverables that their methods never establish.
Matching platform names or repeating client facts earns limited credit when the actual requested workflow remains unanswered.
Additional product dependencies that conflict with explicit procurement exclusions materially reduce credibility.
Adobe claims were assessed for apparent plausibility from the supplied panel only; current product behavior and licensing were not independently verified.
All supplied answers fit their stated word limits; unused space frequently accompanies omitted requirements.
The strongest answers turn university specific needs into named records, test evidence, owners and dated deliverables.
Separate Assets and Real-Time CDP dependencies conflict with explicit purchasing constraints, while extra CJA dependencies need a justified configuration decision.
Several answers replace requested delivery methods with adjacent product capabilities, particularly in consent, identity and reporting.
References to included services adding no hours do not establish a complete effort baseline, and named recovery or rollback documents do not substitute for workable procedures.
